407.title: Q2: which gods hold the body? breath proves itself by leaving (2)
407.hook: the powers of the body brag that they hold it up, and breath settles the argument by starting to walk out
407.tomorrow: Q3: where does breath come from?
407.howItsDone: Breath (prana) is honored in many Hindu practices, from pranayama in yoga to the five pranas offered with the first mouthfuls of a meal in some traditional households.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rayi and prana, matter and breath, the moon and the sun. Your line was the two paths of the sun.

A group project, the night before it's due. Who really carried this? The one who wrote it says the writing. The one who presented says the presentation. The one who booked the room says nobody would've had anywhere to meet. Then the quiet one who did the actual research gets up to leave, and suddenly everyone sees what they were standing on. Bhargava, from Vidarbha, the second student, asks Pippalada: how many gods hold up a living being? Which of them make it shine? Which is greatest? Pippalada answers with exactly that argument.
screen: `WHO REALLY CARRIED THIS?` → `THE QUIET ONE GETS UP TO LEAVE.` → `WHICH GOD IS GREATEST?`

segments.voice: The gods of the body, Pippalada says, are space, wind, fire, water and earth, and speech, mind, the eye and the ear. One day they shine with pride and declare: we hold up this body. We keep it standing. Then breath, prana, the chief of them all, says: don't be deluded. It's me. I divide myself five ways, and I hold it up. They don't believe him. So breath, out of pride, begins to rise, as if to leave. And as he rises, all the others are pulled up with him. When he settles back down, they all settle. The text gives a picture any village would know. When the king bee rises, all the bees rise. When it settles, they all settle. So it was with speech, mind, eye and ear. Then the gods, convinced, sing breath's praises. He burns as fire. He is the sun, the rain, the wind, the earth. He is what is and what isn't, and what never dies. Near the start of this year, in the Chandogya, the powers of the body had the same quarrel, and each one took a turn leaving. Here the story is quicker and sharper. Breath doesn't wait for the others to try. He just begins to stand, and that's enough. Speech, sight and mind are real powers, but they all ride on something none of them can do without. In the story, nobody notices breath until it starts to go.
screen: `SPEECH, MIND, EYE, EAR: WE HOLD IT UP.` · `BREATH: IT'S ME, DIVIDED FIVE WAYS.` · `BREATH RISES; ALL RISE WITH IT.` · `LIKE BEES WITH THEIR KING.` · then, large: `PRANA.`

segments.voice: Breathe normally, and at the top of an in-breath pause for a moment, nothing strained, and see whether everything seems to wait: the thoughts, the listening, the sense of the room. Then let the breath go on, and feel it all start moving again. After two or three, let breath carry the body without your help.
Prana, breath, the chief of the body's powers. Speech, mind, eye and ear all claim to hold the body, until prana begins to leave and they all rise with it.
Your line: when breath left, all left. Tomorrow, a student asks where breath itself comes from. Day four hundred seven, done.

408.title: Q3: where does breath come from? the shadow of the self (3)
408.hook: breath just won the argument; now the third student asks where breath itself comes from, and the answer is a shadow
408.tomorrow: Q4: who sleeps, who dreams, who is awake in sleep?
408.howItsDone: Yoga and Ayurveda teachers still use the names of the five breaths, prana, apana, samana, vyana and udana, from texts like this one, to describe how breath works in the body.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prana, breath, the chief of the body's powers. When breath left, all left, like bees with their king.

Breath has just been crowned. So the next student, Kausalya, son of Ashvala, does what a good student does after a big answer: he asks the question underneath it. Where is breath born from? How does it come into this body, divide itself, and settle? How does it leave? Pippalada's reply begins with a raised eyebrow. You're asking questions beyond questions, he says. But you are devoted to Brahman, so I'll answer. And the answer starts with something you can see on any sunny sidewalk.
screen: `BREATH HAS BEEN CROWNED.` → `WHERE IS BREATH BORN FROM?` → `QUESTIONS BEYOND QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Pippalada says: breath is born from the self. As a shadow falls from a person, so breath is cast from the self. And it comes into this body by the working of the mind. Sit with that picture. A shadow is real. It moves, it has a shape, it can cover a whole wall. But it has no life of its own. Take the person away and the shadow goes too. So breath, the king of yesterday's story, turns out to be the self's shadow: close, faithful, completely dependent. Then the text describes how breath runs the body, like a king telling his officers: you govern these villages, you govern those. The main breath, prana, stays in the eyes and ears, the mouth and nose. Apana, the down-going breath, works in the lower body. Samana, in the middle, carries the food offered into the body evenly, and from it, the text says, rise seven flames. Vyana moves through the channels that branch out from the heart. And udana, the up-going breath, rises through one channel at the end of life and carries a person on: to a good world for good deeds, a painful one for wrongs, and back to the human world for a mix of both. Outside the body, the rising sun is breath too, and the power in the earth steadies the down-going breath. So, back to Kausalya's question beyond questions: where does breath come from? From the self, the way a shadow comes from a person.

segments.voice: Watch the breath move the way you'd watch your shadow walk beside you, going where you go, changing shape. Then gently turn toward what the shadow falls from: the stillness that's aware of breathing. You don't have to find it; just face that way, and let the breath keep moving on its own, close and faithful.
Chaya, a shadow. As a shadow falls from a person, so breath is cast from the self, Pippalada says, and it enters the body by the working of the mind.
Your line: as a shadow. Tomorrow, a student follows the self into sleep. See you then.

409.title: Q4: who sleeps, who dreams, who is awake in sleep? (4)
409.hook: the fourth student asks about bedtime: when you sleep, what goes to sleep, what dreams, and what stays awake?
409.tomorrow: Q5–6: om, and the person of sixteen parts
409.howItsDone: Vedanta teachers often read the Prashna's fourth question alongside the Mandukya's teaching on waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and use sleep as a daily example of awareness that continues without the senses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: chaya, a shadow. Breath, cast from the self the way your shadow is cast from you. Your line was as a shadow.

Last night you did something remarkable, and you don't remember it. You lay down, and the room went away. Then, maybe, you were somewhere else entirely, talking to someone who's been gone for years, in a house that doesn't exist. Then nothing at all, for a while. Then you woke up, and you were you again, with no gap in who you are. Gargya, the Prashna's fourth student, asks about exactly that. What in a person sleeps? What stays awake? Which god sees dreams? Whose is the happiness of deep sleep? And on what does everything rest?
screen: `THE ROOM WENT AWAY.` → `A HOUSE THAT DOESN'T EXIST.` → `WHAT STAYS AWAKE?`

segments.voice: Pippalada starts with a sunset. As the rays of the setting sun all gather back into its disk, and spread out again when it rises, so, when a person sleeps, all the senses gather into the mind. Then that person doesn't hear, see, smell, taste, touch, speak or walk. People say: they're asleep. But not everything sleeps. The fires of breath, Pippalada says, stay awake in this city of the body, tending it all night, like the household fires of a sacrifice. Then dreams. In a dream, the mind, the god of the senses, experiences its own greatness. What it has seen, it sees again. What it has heard, it hears again. Seen and unseen, heard and unheard, real and unreal, it sees them all. Then deep sleep. When the mind is overcome by light, it sees no dreams, and a happiness rises in the body. And an image: as birds go to a tree to rest, so everything goes to rest in the highest self. Then the answer to the last question, what everything rests on. This one, the text says, is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, the doer, the person who is understanding itself. And that one rests in the highest, imperishable self. So who is awake in sleep? Breath, keeping the house. And under it, the one who sees, which never needed eyes to begin with.
screen: `THE SENSES GATHER, LIKE THE SUN'S RAYS.` · `THE FIRES OF BREATH STAY AWAKE.` · `IN DREAMS, THE MIND SEES ALL.` · `BIRDS COME HOME TO A TREE.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO SEES.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let the senses gather in like the sun's rays at sunset: sounds a little farther off, the body's edges softer. Let the mind's pictures come and go while the breath keeps going by itself, like a fire someone else is tending. Rest there, like a bird come home to a tree, and notice that something is still quietly watching.
Q4, the fourth question. Who sleeps, who dreams, who is awake in sleep? The senses sleep in the mind, the mind dreams, breath keeps watch, and the seer rests in the highest self.
Your line: the one who sees. Tomorrow, the last two questions. Day four hundred nine.

410.title: Q5–6: om, and the person of sixteen parts (5–6)
410.hook: the last two students ask about om and about a person made of sixteen parts, and one of them admits he once had to say, I don't know
410.carry: the sixteen parts return to the sea
410.howItsDone: Om is commonly chanted at the start and close of Hindu prayer and study, and some teachers use the Prashna's line about a lie drying a person up to the root when they speak about truthfulness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fourth question, who is awake in sleep. Breath keeps the house, and under it, the one who sees. Today, the Prashna ends.

Sukesha, the sixth student, opens with a story against himself. A prince of Kosala once came to me, he says, and asked: do you know the person of sixteen parts? I said, I don't know. If I knew, why wouldn't I tell you? Whoever speaks what isn't true dries up to the root, so I can't speak falsely. The prince got into his chariot without a word, and left. Now, Sukesha says to Pippalada, I'm asking you. Where is that person?
screen: `DO YOU KNOW THE SIXTEEN PARTS?` → `I DON'T KNOW.` → `A LIE DRIES UP TO THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: First, the fifth question, from Satyakama. What does a person win who meditates on om until the end of life? Pippalada says om is both the higher and the lower Brahman, and its sounds open different worlds. Meditate on one of its three sounds, and you come quickly back to the human world. On two, and you go to the world of the moon, and return. But one who meditates on all three, the whole of om, is freed from wrong the way a snake slips out of its old skin. Then Sukesha's question. Where is the person of sixteen parts? Right here, Pippalada says, inside the body. And he tells how the sixteen arise. The self thought: when I leave, who will leave with me? It made breath. From breath, faith. Then space, wind, light, water, earth, the senses, mind and food. From food, strength. Then discipline, sacred verses, action, the worlds, and finally, name. Sixteen: everything a life is made of. Then an image. As rivers flowing toward the sea reach it and disappear, their names and shapes broken up, and people simply say, the sea, so these sixteen parts reach the person and disappear. Their names are gone. People simply say, the person. And that one is without parts, and deathless. The six students honored Pippalada: you are our father, who carries us across our ignorance to the farther shore. Six questions began with a teacher saying, if we know. They end with students saying, thank you.

segments.voice: Begin where the list of sixteen begins: one breath in, one breath out. Don't hold on to any of it; come back to the breath, and stay there.

411.title: The two knowledges — lower (the Vedas) and higher (that by which the imperishable is grasped) (1.1)
411.hook: a great householder asks for the one thing that, once known, makes everything known, and hears that even the Vedas count as the lower knowledge
411.howItsDone: In traditional Vedic schools students still memorize the Vedas and study the six auxiliary sciences, the vedangas, and Vedanta teachers use the Mundaka's two knowledges to explain why study is a ladder rather than the goal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Prashna's last questions, om and the person of sixteen parts. Your line was the sixteen parts return to the sea. Today, the Mundaka Upanishad begins.
screen: `THE SIXTEEN PARTS RETURN TO THE SEA.`

segments.voice: A library with every book ever written. A whole lifetime in it might get you through one shelf. Then someone walks in and asks the librarian: is there one thing I could know, and then everything else would make sense? That's how the Mundaka opens. Shaunaka, a great householder, comes properly, as a student should, to the sage Angiras, and asks: Sir, what is it that, when it is known, all of this becomes known? And Angiras starts by dividing every kind of knowing in two.
screen: `A LIBRARY OF EVERY BOOK.` → `ONE THING THAT MAKES SENSE OF ALL?` → `SHAUNAKA ASKS ANGIRAS.`

segments.voice: The Mundaka belongs to the Atharva Veda, and it opens with its own family tree. Brahma, first of the gods, taught this knowledge to his eldest son, Atharvan, and it passed teacher to student down to Angiras. Then Shaunaka asks his question, and Angiras says: two knowledges are to be known, so say those who know Brahman. The higher, and the lower. Then the surprise. The lower knowledge is the Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, the Atharva Veda, and with them phonetics, ritual, grammar, the study of words, meter and astronomy, the six sciences that serve the Vedas. All of it: lower. And the higher? That by which the imperishable is grasped. Akshara, the one that doesn't wear away. Notice where this is said. Not by a critic outside the tradition. Inside the Atharva Veda itself, the Veda calls its own recitation the lower knowledge. Shankara reads the lower as knowledge of words and rites, and the higher as the direct knowing the words point to. No one in the story throws the Vedas away. Shaunaka learned them. Angiras learned them. They're the ladder you climb, and the Upanishad is part of the Veda too. The point is what kind of knowing it is. You can know everything about a mango, its region, its chemistry, its price, and never have tasted one. The lower knowledge is everything about. The higher is the taste. And Shaunaka's question has only one kind of answer.
screen: `WHAT, ONCE KNOWN, MAKES ALL KNOWN?` · `TWO KNOWLEDGES: HIGHER AND LOWER.` · `EVEN THE FOUR VEDAS ARE THE LOWER.` · `THE HIGHER GRASPS THE IMPERISHABLE.` · then, large: `PARA AND APARA.`

segments.voice: Think of something you know a lot about, a song, a recipe, a person, and run through the facts you know. Then set the facts aside and remember what it's actually like: the taste, the sound, the feel of being with them. If you'd like, turn toward this moment the same way: not facts about it, just what it's like to be here.
Akshara, the imperishable, what doesn't wear away. In the Mundaka, the lower knowledge is the Vedas and their sciences; the higher is that by which it is grasped.
Your line: two knowledges. Tomorrow, a spider shows how one thing becomes everything. Day four hundred eleven, done.

412.title: The spider and the web; the hair on the body; the plants from the earth (1.1)
412.hook: how does one imperishable thing become a whole world? the Mundaka answers with three pictures from any backyard
412.howItsDone: The spider verse of Mundaka 1.1.7 is a standard teaching text in Vedanta, and teachers of different schools explain it in class to show how they understand the relation between Brahman and the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: akshara, the imperishable. The lower knowledge knows all about; the higher grasps what doesn't wear away. Your line was two knowledges.

Early morning in a garden. Between two branches hangs a web that wasn't there last night, wet with dew, every thread catching light. And near the middle sits its maker, who brought no materials. No wood, no wire, no thread from a store. The whole thing came out of the spider's own body. Angiras has just named the imperishable. The obvious next question: how could one changeless thing turn into everything we see? Instead of a theory, the Mundaka gives three pictures. The first is that spider.
screen: `A WEB THAT WASN'T THERE LAST NIGHT.` → `NO MATERIALS BROUGHT IN.` → `THREE PICTURES.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. Yathorna-nabhih srijate grihnate cha. As a spider sends out its thread and draws it back in. As plants spring up from the earth. As hair grows on the head and body of a living person. So, from the imperishable, everything here comes into being. Each picture teaches something different. The spider: the world doesn't come from some second stuff outside the source. The web is spun from the spider itself, and it can be drawn back in. The plants: the world rises naturally, the way green comes up after rain, without anybody pushing. And the hair grows from a living person without that person thinking about it at all. You don't decide to grow your eyebrows. So the source isn't straining. Then the next verses add: through tapas, that focused heat, Brahman swells, and from it comes food; from food, breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and in action, the deathless. And the one who knows all, whose very tapas is made of knowledge, gives rise to name, form and food. Teachers read the spider differently. Advaita teachers say the web is an appearance, and the spider alone is ultimately real. Ramanuja's school reads the world as truly Brahman's own body, real and dependent. Madhva's school reads Brahman as the independent cause of a world that stays distinct from it. All three keep the spider. Even the Sanskrit word is a small picture: urnanabhi, spider, joins urna, thread or wool, and nabhi, navel.
screen: `AS A SPIDER SPINS AND DRAWS BACK.` · `AS PLANTS RISE FROM THE EARTH.` · `AS HAIR GROWS WITHOUT TRYING.` · `SO, FROM THE IMPERISHABLE, ALL THIS.` · then, large: `URNANABHI.`

segments.voice: Feel your breath go out like a thread and come back in: that's the spider. Notice what grows in you without effort, your hair, your nails, the steady heartbeat, and let thoughts rise and fall on their own, like plants from the ground. Rest at the center, where the thread comes from.
Urnanabhi, the spider. The Mundaka's picture of a world spun from its own source, as naturally as plants from the earth and hair from a living body.
Your line: as the spider. Tomorrow, the Mundaka honors the old fire rites, then calls them boats. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: How can one changeless thing turn into a whole world?
options: Like a spider spinning its web from itself, and drawing it back.
It copies a world it saw somewhere else, piece by piece.
It wears out, and each worn piece becomes a new creature.
chat.meaning: The Mundaka's pictures: as a spider spins its thread and draws it back, as plants rise from earth and hair from a living body, so everything comes from the imperishable.

413.title: Rituals are leaky boats (1.2)
413.hook: the Mundaka praises the fire rites as true, then calls them unsteady boats, and both statements sit side by side in the same chapter
413.tomorrow: go to a teacher, fuel in hand
413.howItsDone: Hindu households keep daily and seasonal rites, from lighting a lamp to fire offerings (homa), and Vedanta teachers explain this passage as a lesson about what rites can reach, not a call to stop them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: urnanabhi, the spider, spinning its web from itself and drawing it back. Your line was as the spider.

A rowboat can be a perfectly good boat. It'll take you around the lake, out to the dock, across to the picnic spot. Now try to cross an ocean in it. Nothing about the boat has changed. What changed is where you're trying to go. The second section of the Mundaka does something bold with that idea. It's talking about the great fire rites of the Vedas. First, it honors them. Then it calls them boats, and tells you what kind.
screen: `A GOOD ROWBOAT.` → `NOW CROSS AN OCEAN IN IT.` → `THE RITES ARE BOATS.`

segments.voice: The section opens with a clear yes. This is the truth, it says: the rites the sages saw in the sacred verses are spread out in many ways. Practice them faithfully. This is your path to the world of good deeds. Then it describes the fire offering in loving detail, the seven flickering tongues of flame, each with a name: the black one, the terrible, the swift as thought, the deep red, the smoky, the sparkling, the one of every shape. Then the turn. Plava hy ete adridha yajnarupah. Unsteady, indeed, are these boats, the eighteen forms of sacrifice. Fools who praise them as the highest good go again and again to old age and death. Thinking themselves wise, they wander like the blind led by the blind. They enjoy the heaven their good works earned, and when it runs out, they come back down. So which is it? Are the rites true, or leaky? The Mundaka says both, on purpose. The rites really do what they promise: they earn a good world. But a good world is still a world that ends. They're boats for the lake, not the ocean. Then the line that explains the whole section: the uncreated is not won by what is made. Nasty akritah kritena. Nothing you build, however holy, can build your way to the unbuilt. Different schools weighed this differently. The Mimamsa tradition held ritual itself as the heart of the Veda. Vedanta teachers read this passage as the turn toward knowledge. Others keep the rites and the inner search side by side.
screen: `FIRST: THE RITES ARE TRUE.` · `SEVEN TONGUES OF FLAME.` · `THEN: UNSTEADY BOATS.` · `THE UNMADE ISN'T WON BY THE MADE.` · then, large: `PLAVA HY ETE ADRIDHA.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you do faithfully, a ritual or routine that's good for you, and honor it for a breath: it works, it carries you. Then ask gently where it's carrying you, and whether there's somewhere it can't go, without answering quickly. Then let the question go and sit for a moment, nothing made, nothing earned.
Plava, an unsteady boat. The Mundaka honors the fire rites as true, then calls them unsteady boats: they earn good worlds, but the uncreated isn't won by what's made.
Your line: the boat leaks. That's week fifty-nine: breath leaves, a shadow, awake in sleep, sixteen parts, two knowledges, the spider, and the leaky boats. Day four hundred thirteen.
screen: `WEEK FIFTY-NINE: BREATH · SHADOW · SLEEP · SIXTEEN PARTS · TWO KNOWLEDGES · THE SPIDER · THE BOATS`

chat.says: Does the Mundaka say the old fire rites are useless?
options: No. It calls them true; they earn a good world, but one that ends.
Yes. It says they never worked, so the priests should stop.
Yes. It says only the eighteen priests may still perform them.
chat.meaning: The Mundaka first calls the rites true, a path to a world of good deeds, then unsteady boats: that world ends, and the uncreated isn't won by the made.
